venueDescription: Bellever’s riverbank gives families one of the easier ways to enjoy the East Dart without heading deep onto the moor. A surfaced path leads from the car park towards the river, with picnic spots, benches, forest trails and Bellever Tor nearby if the visit stretches beyond the water. The river edge is the draw here: paddling, stones, shade from the trees and that open Dartmoor feeling without being far from the car. Ponies often graze alongside it, making for a beautiful setting for a picnic, afternoon by the water, or family dip. Being Dartmoor, the water levels and weather can change quickly, and there are deep spots right new to shallower sections, so it's definitely worth keeping an additionally close eye and it can get busy in the summer months on hotter days owing to the easy access and toilet facilities within the car park. There isn't much shade along the river, and while it is possible to cross over onto a larger stretch of grass, it's not the simplest crossing if you're loaded up or having very little people in tow, so be sure to arrive early on hot days to find a good spot.

venueDescription:
Newton Abbot Museum is set inside the restored Victorian church at Newton’s Place, with local history, railway stories, market heritage, changing exhibitions and hands-on displays. It has the kind of scale that makes it easy to drop into without turning it into a longer trip if you don't have time, but there is enough for children to slow down, look closely and follow their own interests. The railway exhibits are the headline draw — a full-scale working signal box with real levers children can pull, a model atmospheric railway, a railway carriage and displays on Brunel's plans for the South Devon Railway, including the story of how rats gnawing through leather seals helped bring the whole system down. Beyond the railway there are recreated rooms including an Iron Age hut, a Victorian parlour and a 1940s war room, plus hands-on activities including designing an Aller Vale pot, sending codes on the signal bells, trying on historical hats and feeling the difference between rich and poor Victorian fabrics. There are over 20 interactive activities in total. A hidden bird hunt around the museum is a reliable hit with younger children. The museum also runs drop-in family craft sessions and workshops alongside its changing exhibitions — worth checking the calendar before visiting.

The museum is pushchair-accessible, with a lift to all levels, ramps through the main gallery, sensory bags, ear defenders, activity sheets and baby changing available. It is a useful indoor anchor for a Newton Abbot town visit, with cafés, shops and the bus station nearby.

venueDescription:
Seaton Wetlands is one of the easiest places in East Devon to make wildlife feel accessible for children, with level trails, boardwalks, bird hides, pond-dipping platforms and wide estuary views across the Axe Valley. The reserve is made up of several connected wetland areas, including Seaton Marshes, Black Hole Marsh, Colyford Common and Stafford Marsh, each offering something slightly different to discover. Black Hole Marsh is a particular highlight for birdwatching, with lagoons, viewing hides and opportunities to spot wading birds and other wildlife throughout the seasons.

The appeal is in slowing down and noticing things in a fairly low-effort, low-key way: birds moving across the water, dragonflies in warmer months, reeds, mudflats and little changes in the landscape as you explore. The generally flat paths make much of the reserve manageable for families with pushchairs, balance bikes and young cyclists, although cycling access varies between sections. Children can enjoy peering through viewing windows, spotting wildlife from the hides or following the trails between different habitats, while older children with an interest in birds, nature or photography will find plenty to keep them engaged. There's enough variety to make a longer outing of it, but it's equally lovely for a shorter wander without needing to cover the whole reserve.

venueDescription: The oldest public open space in England, laid out in 1612, which is a fact worth telling older children before you arrive because it changes how they look at the place. Set just behind the High Street beside Rougemont Castle, the gardens are free, open from early morning until dusk and make a natural breathing space in the middle of a city visit without needing to go anywhere. What gives Northernhay its particular character is the way the everyday park; lawns, paths, flowerbeds, benches — sits right up against visible stretches of Roman and Saxon city wall that are genuinely ancient and touchable. Sculptures are scattered throughout, including the 1878 Deer Stalker and the 1923 War Memorial by local sculptor John Angel, and children who like history trails will find the Exeter history information boards a good thread to follow around the garden. Local legend has it the gardens were also used for witch hangings in the 1800s, which might be interesting to certain older children with a history fascination.

venueDescription: A pottery painting studio, lifestyle store and café on Station Road in Totnes that includes considerably more than a standard pottery café. The ceramic studio is the biggest of its kind in the South West, with hundreds of pieces to choose from; everything from fairy tale figures and robots to mugs, bowls and dog bowls that can be painted with professional glazes that are then kiln-fired and either collected or posted home. Everything is individually priced, so there's usually something for each budget. For families who won't be around long enough to collect, there's also a Paint & Go option using poster paints where children take their piece home the same day, which is worth knowing about before you choose your ceramic. It's not a small or quiet setting; two floors of painting tables that feel fairly busy as the pottery studio is situated within the wider store area and nearby to the Deli & Kitchen, but the sheer variety of choice is the main draw if you've got a creative child with something very specific in mind to paint.

venueDescription: A small urban woodland tucked into the Withycombe Raleigh part of Exmouth, managed by the Wild East Devon rangers as a community nature reserve and one of the more quietly pleasant green spaces in the town for children who like poking about in trees rather than heading straight for the beach. The reserve acts as a wildlife corridor through the town, with winding paths through woodland and scrub, butterflies in season and the kind of unhurried, slightly wild feel that's harder to find than it should be in a seaside town. Free to enter year-round, and accessible from both the railway and bus station without needing a car.

venueDescription: A small but charming 7.25-inch gauge miniature railway tucked into the award-winning gardens behind Buckfastleigh station, run by volunteers alongside the South Devon heritage railway. The ride is a half-mile loop through flower borders and woodland that loops it's way around the station car park. It's gentle, short and perfectly pitched at younger children who love trains but won't sit still for a full heritage steam journey but would love the excitment of a ride. The locomotive is a diesel named Greenie, well-maintained and much-loved by its volunteer crew and it's the kind of simple thing that makes a Buckfastleigh morning feel complete rather than rushed — the gardens have picnic benches alongside the miniature railway station, which gives parents somewhere to settle while children watch, play or wait for another go. The station itself has a café, toilets and a children's play area, and the Otter and Butterfly Sanctuary is a two-minute walk away, making the two a natural pairing. The miniature railway runs every weekend (weather-dependant) between April and October but this can (very occasionally) miss a week, so it's worth double-checking ahead for a specific date if it's a special occasion and the visit is centred on a ride.

venueDescription: A small, remote and genuinely beautiful sandy bay just south of Start Point in the South Hams, accessible via a 10–15 minute walk down a steep path from the Start Point car park. At low tide the beach opens out with fine sand, rock pools along the fringes, a small stream, boulders to climb and caves to explore. The water is clear and calm in settled weather, making it good for swimming and paddleboarding in summer, and seals are regularly spotted from the beach and nearby rocks. The sense of having found somewhere special makes the walk worthwhile, but the steep path and no-facilities situation means it's genuinely one for prepared families who are comfortable carrying what they need and setting up for the day, rather than spontaneous visits. Low tide significantly changes how much beach there is to use, and the coastal path setting gives older children more of a sense of discovery, making it a brilliant option for a slightly more varied and interesting beach trip. There are no lifeguards and there's no café at the beach so stock up on snacks - and while there are basic porta-cabin toilets at the car park, these close early so plan ahead.

venueDescription: Cherry Brook is a wilder Dartmoor river spot with plenty of stretches of shallow water right alongside the open moorland. It is a beautiful spot for a picnic, or a quiet paddle, and being one of the lesser known spots it's rarely crowded. It's informal, slightly uneven grass and much more rustic than many river spots, but with Dartmoor ponies often grazing nearby, and access to the Bellever circular route from the car park, it can work well as a quick stop at the end of a walk, or as a visit in its own right if you're looking for somewhere to cool off. With hard-standing parking directly across the road, it doesn't feel like a big effort to stop and enjoy a break by the stream, and the slower, shallow water in summer months means it's well suited to smaller children and inexperienced river waders! It's worth noting that there isn't much shade, so do plan ahead in the heat.
